justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon were based on the underlying trend in the data, alongside short- and medium-term factors that are expected to influence outcomes. For the one-day forecast, the point estimate of 53.15 reflects a combination of very recent observations and short-term dynamics, such as momentum or immediate events that have limited time to fully play out. At the one-week horizon, the point estimate of 53.5 was influenced by the expectation of some stabilization or modest continuation of the trend, as weekly movement typically accounts for slightly longer-term influences, like recurrent patterns or emerging market factors. By the one-month horizon, the point estimate of 54.2 incorporates both the cumulative effect of the recent trend and broader structural factors that are expected to manifest over a longer time frame, though with increasing uncertainty as forecasts extend further into the future.

The widths of the confidence intervals at each horizon are shaped by different layers of uncertainty. For the one-day horizon, the narrower interval (52.0 to 54.3) reflects relatively low uncertainty because short timeframes are less sensitive to compounding random shocks and are more informed by the most recent data. For the one-week interval, uncertainty widens (50.8 to 56.2) as there is more time for unexpected factors—like minor news events or short-term volatility—to affect the outcomes. The one-month horizon has the widest interval (49.5 to 58.9) due to its susceptibility to more significant structural changes or major unforeseen disruptions that could develop over weeks. In general, uncertainty grows with time as forecasts rely on longer extrapolations and are influenced by a larger range of possible external influences.

There are always risks or events that could push outcomes outside these intervals, though they are generally expected to be rare. For example, an unexpected geopolitical crisis, an economic shock, or unpredictable policy changes could cause the actual outcomes to land far from these estimates, particularly at the one-week or one-month horizons. Similarly, highly unusual but possible events—such as statistical anomalies or unprecedented market behavior—introduce the small risk of extreme outcomes. While the confidence intervals aim to capture 90% of the likely range, these "black swan" scenarios fall into the remaining 10%, where outcomes move beyond the anticipated range due to highly unusual or unexpected conditions.
